title: Council members take oath of office - NewsBreak
text:
By JILL ZIMA BORSKI ,
5 hours ago
MARATHON — The city of Marathon swore in a new council Nov. 18. Residents elected newcomer Debra Struyf last month along with incumbents Lynn Landry and Robyn Still. They are to serve three-year terms.
Jeff Smith, a former bank executive, was not re-elected. He was thanked “for making great contributions to the city of Marathon over the years” and was bestowed a plant from the city.
Council members Kenny Matlock and Lynny del Gaizo were not up for re-election and continue their council terms. Matlock was nominated for mayor but declined, saying, “I don’t think I have the time,” adding that others may be better at the role’s social obligations. The council then chose Del Gaizo as mayor and Matlock nominated Struyf as vice mayor. She was confirmed by the council’s vote.
Next, the city’s wastewater needs arose. The council approved a not-to-exceed amount of $60,000 for emergency cleaning of three injection wells at its wastewater treatment plant along with a contract for a deep injection well transmission main project awarded to Coral Construction Company in an amount not to exceed $2,454,750, with a completion deadline of December 2028. The city maintained that while a deep injection well is expensive, the new system will eliminate nutrients, and prevent pharmaceuticals and "forever chemicals" from being introduced into Keys waters.
The city then approved several grant agreements with the Monroe County Tourist Development Council for Coco Plum and Sombrero Beach cleaning, Oceanfront Dog Park renovations and installation of the children’s splash-pad, restroom and concession stand.
The city also approved a contract between the city and Discount Rock & Sand Inc. in an amount not to exceed $459,982 for construction of pickleball courts and associated improvements such as lighting and water service at Oceanfront Park using funds from its capital infrastructure budget.
The agenda item said the city desired to construct new pickleball courts to meet the demand of the fast-growing popular sport. The plans were prepared in house and put out to bid. Four contractors responded with bids. The lowest cost submitted was from Sports Surfaces LLC in the amount of $345,480. However, the city determined their bid was not responsive because no cost was provided for the required bonds, its cost for electric work was extremely low and it appeared to have substituted lights with an unknown brand.
Additionally, the city discussed its desire to secure grant funding by using lobbyists in addition to its own efforts to procure funding from national and state sources for several projects. At the federal level, Marathon’s focus is to continue acquisition of funds through the Florida Keys Water Quality Improvement Program (FKWQIP). Funding for these programs has been lucrative in the past several years with its current lobbying team in place. Last year, with a change in administrations, the Keys received no FKWQIP funding, said council documentation.
City staff will work to obtain maximal funding through the infrastructure bill that was made available by Congress. Focused on coastal sustainability, funds are becoming available for major infrastructure improvements, the city wrote. Through this and other sources, including FKWQIP, the city will be working to fund construction of the required deep well via grants. One more city goal is to support additional funding for the National Marine Sanctuary program and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary in light of current issues involving significant coral loss.
Marathon’s city council next meets Dec. 9.
